title: TEDx Stage: Build Your Narrative
description: You've been selected to deliver a TEDx-style talk at your school's annual innovation summit. Over 12 weeks, craft a powerful narrative, master persuasive speaking, conquer stage fright, handle tough audience questions, and build influence through the art of storytelling. This is your stage — own it.
how_to_play: You have 12 weeks to prepare and deliver a TEDx-style talk at your school.
Each round presents a decision about narrative structure, rehearsal, audience engagement, or influence strategy.
Watch your dashboard — Narrative Architecture, Performance Mastery, Audience Psychology, and Influence Building are interconnected.
NPCs like Coach TED, the Judge Panel, and your Rival Speaker will react to your choices.
Crises like harsh critiques and imposter syndrome will test your resilience.
Balance depth with delivery — a brilliant script means nothing if you can't perform it, and charisma alone won't cover shallow content.
learning_objectives: Understand narrative psychology and story structure (hero's journey, tension arcs)
Practice persuasive communication techniques and rhetorical devices
Develop emotional intelligence for connecting with diverse audiences
Learn to manage performance anxiety and build stage confidence
Build influence through authentic storytelling and vulnerability
Analyze audience psychology and adapt messaging in real time
Master pitch frameworks used by world-class speakers
cultural_context: School TEDx culture, youth voice movements, storytelling traditions across cultures, modern communication skills

tick_rules.label: Authenticity Attracts
tick_rules.description: Authentic vulnerability builds genuine audience connection over time.

tick_rules.label: Influence Momentum

interactions.label: Overconfidence Gap
interactions.description: High influence without vulnerability comes across as arrogant — audiences disengage.

interactions.label: Stage Presence Amplifies Message
interactions.description: Confident delivery makes your arguments more convincing.

interactions.label: Story Resonance
interactions.description: A well-crafted narrative naturally draws audiences in.

interactions.label: Style Over Substance Risk
interactions.description: Over-rehearsing shallow content makes the talk feel polished but hollow.

behaviors.message: Your story structure needs work. Remember: every great talk has a clear through-line. What's the ONE idea you want the audience to remember?
You need to rehearse more! The best speakers practice until the words feel like breathing. Let's run through it again.
Now THAT's a talk! You've got substance AND delivery. The audience won't know what hit them!
That moment of vulnerability — that's where the magic is. Don't edit it out. Audiences connect with real, not perfect.
Your claims lack evidence. Where are your sources? A TEDx talk must be grounded in facts, not just feelings.
The judges confer and deliver a harsh verdict: 'You're rehearsed but robotic. We don't feel anything. Where's YOUR story in all this?' The critique stings but exposes a real gap.
The panel nods approvingly: 'This is TEDx-caliber work. Compelling argument, clear structure, real conviction. Well done.'
Your rival posts a slick teaser video of their talk prep. The comments section is buzzing. The pressure is on.

Your rival casually mentions they've already given talks at two other schools. 'Don't worry, you'll do fine,' they say with a smile that doesn't reach their eyes. Doubt creeps in — do you actually belong on this stage?
Your rival catches your rehearsal and goes quiet. Later they text: 'Okay, I'll admit it — your talk gave me chills. This is going to be a real competition.'

rounds.situation: The TEDx committee has approved your application! Now comes the hardest part: what will you talk about? A great TEDx talk starts with ONE powerful idea worth spreading. Your coach wants to know your direction.
rounds.goal: Select the core topic and angle for your TEDx talk.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: The best talks aren't about the biggest topics — they're about a unique angle on a universal truth.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What personal experience gives you a unique perspective that nobody else could share?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Teenager brainstorming at desk with sticky notes, mind map on wall, notebook open, school TEDx poster visible, warm lighting, semi-realistic

choices.label: A. A Personal Failure That Changed Everything
choices.description: Build your talk around a deeply personal story of failure and transformation. Raw, vulnerable, and relatable.
choices.feedback: Bold choice! Personal stories are the backbone of the most-watched TED talks. Brene Brown's vulnerability talk has 60M+ views for a reason.

skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.
skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.
skill_explanation.creativity: Combining ideas in unexpected ways shows innovative thinking.

choices.label: B. A Data-Driven Argument for Change
choices.description: Pick a social issue and build an evidence-based case. Facts, figures, and a call to action.
choices.feedback: The Hans Rosling approach! Data-driven talks change minds because they challenge assumptions with evidence.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Resisting the quick fix in favor of lasting results shows maturity.

choices.label: C. A Live Demonstration or Experiment
choices.description: Design your talk around a live demo — building something, conducting an experiment, or creating art on stage.
choices.feedback: High risk, high reward! Live demos can be unforgettable — or disastrous. Think of the best product launches you've seen.

skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Evaluating risk vs. reward is a key life skill.
skill_explanation.creativity: Not settling for the obvious solution builds creative problem-solving.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: D. A Contrarian Take on a Popular Belief
choices.description: Challenge something everyone assumes is true. Provoke, debate, and reframe thinking.
choices.feedback: Controversial ideas get attention, but you'll need rock-solid logic and thick skin. The best contrarian talks change paradigms.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Taking a calculated risk shows you can handle uncertainty.
skill_explanation.creativity: Thinking outside the box leads to more original solutions.

rounds.situation: Coach TED says your topic is promising, but the structure is a mess. 'A great talk is like a great building — it needs architecture,' they say. Time to choose your narrative framework.
rounds.goal: Select the storytelling framework for your talk.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Structure is invisible when done well, but its absence is painfully obvious. Choose a framework that serves your idea.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Think of a talk or story that captivated you — what made it impossible to stop listening?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Whiteboard with narrative arc diagrams, teenager and coach planning story structure, markers and sticky notes, school setting, semi-realistic

choices.label: A. The Hero's Journey
choices.description: Classic three-act structure: ordinary world, challenge, transformation. Timeless and emotionally powerful.
choices.feedback: The oldest storytelling structure in human history — and still the most powerful. Joseph Campbell would approve.

skill_explanation.creativity: Exploring an unconventional approach shows creative thinking.
skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.

choices.label: B. Problem-Solution-Vision
choices.description: Start with the problem, present your solution, end with the vision of a better world. Clear and persuasive.
choices.feedback: The consultant's framework! Clean, logical, and action-oriented. Great for policy and social change talks.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Waiting for the right moment instead of rushing shows self-control.

choices.label: C. Nested Stories (Russian Doll)
choices.description: Weave multiple short stories that all connect to one central theme. Complex but mesmerizing when done right.
choices.feedback: Ambitious! Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's 'Danger of a Single Story' uses this beautifully. But it demands precise timing and transitions.

skill_explanation.creativity: Looking at the problem from a new angle demonstrates creativity.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Stepping outside your comfort zone builds risk assessment skills.

choices.label: D. Build-Break-Build (Tension Loops)
choices.description: Create tension, break it with a reveal, build again. Like a thriller — keep the audience on the edge.
choices.feedback: The suspense master's approach! Great speakers use tension loops to make audiences lean forward in their seats.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.
skill_explanation.creativity: Combining ideas in unexpected ways shows innovative thinking.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: Your structure is taking shape, but Coach TED pushes back: 'Where's the evidence? A talk without research is just an opinion.' The Judge Panel wants to see credible sources.
rounds.coaching_moment: Delayed gratification: Research is invisible labor. The audience won't see your hours in the library, but they'll feel the depth.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How do you know when you've researched enough to speak with authority on a topic?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Teenager in school library surrounded by books and laptop, taking notes, research papers spread out, focused concentration, semi-realistic

choices.label: A. Academic Deep Dive
choices.description: Read published studies, cite researchers, and build an evidence-based argument. Slow but bulletproof.
choices.feedback: Rigorous! Academic research gives your talk unshakeable credibility. The judges will respect this foundation.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Prioritizing long-term gains over short-term comfort builds character.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. Interview Real People
choices.description: Talk to experts, affected communities, and everyday people. First-hand stories add emotional depth.
choices.feedback: Human-centered research! Real voices make abstract problems concrete. This is how journalists build compelling narratives.

skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.
skill_explanation.creativity: Not settling for the obvious solution builds creative problem-solving.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. Conduct Your Own Experiment
choices.description: Design a small experiment or survey at school. Original data nobody else has — risky but unique.
choices.feedback: Original research at 14! Even a simple school survey gives you data that no other speaker has. Bold move.

skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Being willing to try something uncertain develops risk tolerance.
skill_explanation.creativity: Thinking outside the box leads to more original solutions.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Multimedia Research Collage
choices.description: Gather videos, podcasts, social media posts, and news clips. Build a modern multimedia evidence base.
choices.feedback: Digital-native approach! Multimedia research reflects how your generation actually consumes information.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.
skill_explanation.creativity: Exploring an unconventional approach shows creative thinking.

rounds.situation: Coach TED sits you down: 'Your talk has structure and facts. But where are YOU in this? The audience doesn't just want information — they want to connect with a human being. How much of yourself are you willing to share?'
rounds.goal: Decide how much personal vulnerability to include in your talk.
rounds.coaching_moment: Empathy: Vulnerability is not weakness — it's the courage to be seen. But it must be purposeful, not performative.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Is there a difference between being vulnerable and oversharing? Where's the line?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Teenager sitting across from speaking coach in quiet room, emotional conversation, warm lighting, supportive atmosphere, semi-realistic

choices.label: A. Go All In — Share Your Deepest Struggle
choices.description: Share a deeply personal experience — failure, fear, or a moment that shaped you. Maximum vulnerability.
choices.feedback: The bravest choice. Brene Brown says vulnerability is the birthplace of innovation, creativity, and change. This will resonate deeply.

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.
skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Not always playing it safe helps you grow as a decision-maker.

choices.label: B. Strategic Vulnerability — One Curated Story
choices.description: Share one carefully chosen personal moment that perfectly illustrates your point. Controlled but authentic.
choices.feedback: Smart and effective. The best speakers are selectively vulnerable — they share what serves the talk's message.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.
skill_explanation.creativity: Looking at the problem from a new angle demonstrates creativity.

choices.label: C. Use Others' Stories Instead of Yours
choices.description: Tell someone else's compelling story. Lower personal risk, but the audience may not connect as deeply.
choices.feedback: Safe and effective if the stories are powerful. But the judges may notice you're hiding behind others' experiences.

skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: D. Use Humor as Your Vulnerability
choices.description: Be self-deprecating and funny. Humor disarms audiences and creates connection without heavy emotion.
choices.feedback: The comedian's approach! Humor is a powerful connection tool, but make sure it serves your message, not deflects from it.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.
skill_explanation.creativity: Combining ideas in unexpected ways shows innovative thinking.
skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

rounds.situation: It's time for your first complete run-through. Coach TED has booked the school auditorium for an evening session. Your palms are sweating, your heart is racing. This is the first time you'll say the whole thing out loud, start to finish.
rounds.goal: Choose your rehearsal strategy for maximum improvement.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: The first full rehearsal is always humbling. Great speakers embrace the cringe and learn from it.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do most people avoid practicing in front of others? What are they really afraid of?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Teenager on empty school auditorium stage, single spotlight, practicing alone, notes in hand, nervous energy, semi-realistic

choices.label: A. Solo Practice with Video Recording
choices.description: Rehearse alone, record yourself, and watch it back. Painful but private — you control the feedback loop.
choices.feedback: Self-review is powerful! Seeing yourself on camera reveals habits you never noticed — the ums, the fidgeting, the pacing.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Choosing a future benefit over an immediate reward shows patience.
skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: B. Rehearse for 3 Trusted Friends
choices.description: Invite your closest friends to watch and give honest feedback. A small, safe audience.
choices.feedback: Smart! A small trusted audience simulates real conditions while keeping the stakes manageable. Their reactions tell you what works.

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.
skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. Present to the Entire Class
choices.description: Go big — present to 30+ classmates. Maximum exposure, maximum feedback, maximum nerves.
choices.feedback: Brave! Nothing simulates TEDx pressure like a real audience. Some will love it, some will be brutally honest. Both are gold.

skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Evaluating risk vs. reward is a key life skill.
skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.
skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.

choices.label: D. Intensive 1-on-1 with Coach TED
choices.description: Spend the evening with your coach, going line by line. Deep technique work — slower but more precise.
choices.feedback: The masterclass approach! One-on-one coaching polishes your technique, but you miss the experience of facing a real crowd.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Investing effort now for later payoff builds discipline.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: Midpoint check: your talk has heart, but does it have punch? Coach TED introduces you to the ancient art of rhetoric. 'Aristotle had three tools: logos, ethos, pathos. Which will you lead with?'
rounds.goal: Strengthen the persuasive power of your talk.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Persuasion isn't manipulation — it's helping people see a truth they haven't considered.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What's the difference between persuading someone and manipulating them?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Ancient Greek pillars blending with modern school stage, teenager studying rhetoric notes, Aristotle quote on screen, dramatic composition, semi-realistic

choices.label: A. Lead with Logos (Logic & Evidence)
choices.description: Stack your argument with data, logic chains, and undeniable evidence. Make it impossible to disagree.
choices.feedback: The scientist's weapon! Logos appeals to the rational mind. If your evidence is strong, your argument becomes nearly unassailable.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Resisting the quick fix in favor of lasting results shows maturity.

choices.label: B. Lead with Pathos (Emotion & Story)
choices.description: Make the audience FEEL before they think. Use vivid imagery, emotional stories, and sensory language.
choices.feedback: The storyteller's power! Neuroscience shows that emotions drive decisions — logic justifies them after. You're speaking to the heart.

skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.
skill_explanation.creativity: Not settling for the obvious solution builds creative problem-solving.

choices.label: C. Lead with Ethos (Credibility & Authority)
choices.description: Establish yourself as someone worth listening to. Reference your experience, mentors, and track record.
choices.feedback: Credibility first! 'Why should I listen to this 14-year-old?' If you answer that question early, everything else lands harder.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Taking a calculated risk shows you can handle uncertainty.

choices.label: D. Lead with Kairos (Perfect Timing & Relevance)
choices.description: Connect your talk to RIGHT NOW — current events, trending topics, what everyone is already talking about.
choices.feedback: Relevance is power! When your talk feels timely and urgent, the audience thinks 'This matters to me, RIGHT NOW.' That's the kairos effect.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.
skill_explanation.creativity: Thinking outside the box leads to more original solutions.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Coach TED shows you a video of your last rehearsal. 'Your words are strong, but your body is telling a different story. You're pacing, fidgeting, and barely making eye contact. Let's fix your stage presence.'
rounds.goal: Develop your physical stage presence and delivery technique.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Your body language communicates before your words do. Great speakers align body and message.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Have you ever believed someone's words but felt something was off? That's incongruent body language.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Teenager practicing power poses and gestures on stage with coach watching, mirror on side, stage lighting, movement arrows drawn, semi-realistic

choices.label: A. Master Movement & Power Positions
choices.description: Learn to own the stage physically — purposeful walking, power stances, strategic positioning for emphasis.
choices.feedback: Stage geometry! The TED red circle is famous — great speakers use physical space to emphasize their message. Power positions project confidence.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.
skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: B. Eye Contact & Audience Scanning
choices.description: Practice the 'lighthouse technique' — slowly sweeping eye contact across all sections. Connection through the eyes.
choices.feedback: Eyes are the gateway! Studies show that speakers who maintain eye contact are rated 30% more trustworthy and persuasive.

skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.
skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: C. Vocal Mastery — Pace, Pause, Power
choices.description: Train your voice: dramatic pauses, volume shifts, pacing changes. The voice is your primary instrument.
choices.feedback: The pause is the speaker's most powerful tool. When you stop talking, the audience leans in. Vocal variety keeps them engaged.

skill_explanation.creativity: Exploring an unconventional approach shows creative thinking.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Waiting for the right moment instead of rushing shows self-control.

choices.label: D. Forget Technique — Be Naturally You
choices.description: Stop trying to perform and just BE yourself on stage. Authenticity over polish. Conversation, not presentation.
choices.feedback: The anti-technique technique! Some of the best TED talks feel like a friend telling you a story. But 'natural' on stage is itself a skill that takes practice.

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.
skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.
skill_explanation.creativity: Looking at the problem from a new angle demonstrates creativity.

rounds.situation: Disaster strikes during a school-wide preview: the projector dies mid-slide, a phone rings in the audience, and you forget your opening line. Coach TED says: 'This is actually the best thing that could have happened. How you handle chaos defines you as a speaker.'
rounds.goal: Develop resilience strategies for when things go wrong on stage.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Professional speakers don't avoid disasters — they prepare for them. The audience respects grace under pressure more than perfection.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do we admire people who handle unexpected problems well? What does it reveal about their character?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Teenager on stage with broken projector screen, audience watching expectantly, moment of decision, dramatic lighting, school auditorium, semi-realistic

choices.label: A. Improv Comedy Training
choices.description: Take improv classes to build quick-thinking and comfort with the unexpected. 'Yes, and...' becomes your superpower.
choices.feedback: Improv is the speaker's secret weapon! When you can think on your feet, nothing that goes wrong can truly derail you.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.
skill_explanation.creativity: Combining ideas in unexpected ways shows innovative thinking.
skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: B. Build a Bulletproof Backup Plan
choices.description: Prepare for every possible failure: memorize your talk without slides, have backup equipment, create a 'disaster protocol.'
choices.feedback: The professional's approach! Top speakers have their talk memorized so well they could deliver it in a blackout.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Prioritizing long-term gains over short-term comfort builds character.

choices.label: C. Lean Into the Chaos — Make It Part of the Show
choices.description: When things break, use it. 'Well, I guess the universe wants me to tell this part without slides...' Turn disasters into moments.
choices.feedback: The jazz musician's approach! The best live moments are unscripted. When you embrace chaos with grace, the audience falls in love with you.

skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Stepping outside your comfort zone builds risk assessment skills.
skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.
skill_explanation.creativity: Not settling for the obvious solution builds creative problem-solving.

choices.label: D. Prevention Over Recovery — Eliminate All Variables
choices.description: Obsessively control the environment: arrive early, check all tech, have a stage manager, eliminate surprises.
choices.feedback: Control what you can control! But remember — you can't prevent everything, and over-controlling can make you rigid.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Choosing a future benefit over an immediate reward shows patience.

rounds.situation: The TEDx event is three weeks away. Coach TED asks the critical question: 'Who exactly is in that audience? Teachers, students, parents, maybe a local journalist. What do they NEED to hear from you?'
rounds.goal: Adapt your talk to connect with your specific audience.
rounds.coaching_moment: Empathy: Great communication isn't about what you want to say — it's about what your audience needs to hear.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How does the same message need to change depending on who's listening?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Teenager creating audience persona cards on table, sticky notes with different faces and labels, strategy planning, school library, semi-realistic

choices.label: A. Speak Directly to Your Peers
choices.description: Make it relatable to 13-14 year olds. Use their language, their references, their struggles. If they feel it, everyone else will too.
choices.feedback: Know your core audience! When peers connect with your message, the energy in the room becomes electric.

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.
skill_explanation.creativity: Thinking outside the box leads to more original solutions.

choices.label: B. Find the Universal Human Thread
choices.description: Identify the theme that transcends age — love, fear, belonging, growth. Make everyone in the room see themselves in your story.
choices.feedback: The master communicator's choice! Universal themes make your talk timeless. A 14-year-old and a 50-year-old both understand what it means to feel like an outsider.

skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.
skill_explanation.creativity: Exploring an unconventional approach shows creative thinking.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. Challenge the Adults in the Room
choices.description: Flip the script — use your youth as your authority. 'You think you know what our generation faces? Let me show you.' Bold and provocative.
choices.feedback: The Greta Thunberg approach! When young people speak truth to power, it's electrifying. But make sure your facts are bulletproof.

skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Being willing to try something uncertain develops risk tolerance.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. Make It Interactive — Involve the Audience
choices.description: Add audience participation: polls, show-of-hands, pair discussions. Turn your talk into a shared experience.
choices.feedback: High engagement, high risk! Interactive elements can make your talk unforgettable — or chaotically derail it. Timing is everything.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Not always playing it safe helps you grow as a decision-maker.
skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.

rounds.situation: Two weeks to go. Your talk is nearly ready, but Coach TED says: 'A TEDx talk doesn't start on stage — it starts before you walk out. Build anticipation. Create buzz. Make people WANT to be in that room.'
rounds.goal: Build pre-event influence and anticipation for your talk.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: In the attention economy, the best ideas don't win — the best-marketed ideas do. Your talk needs an audience before it starts.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Is marketing your ideas the same as selling out? Where's the line between promotion and substance?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Teenager creating social media content for TEDx talk, phone and laptop, designing promotional poster, school hallway with TEDx banners, semi-realistic

choices.label: A. Launch a Social Media Campaign
choices.description: Create a teaser series: behind-the-scenes prep, mini-clips, countdown posts. Build a following before the event.
choices.feedback: Digital amplification! A social media campaign can double your audience impact. But don't let content creation eat into rehearsal time.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.
skill_explanation.creativity: Looking at the problem from a new angle demonstrates creativity.

choices.label: B. Strategic Word-of-Mouth — Plant Seeds
choices.description: Tell key influencers (popular students, teachers, student council) about your topic. Let curiosity spread naturally.
choices.feedback: The grassroots approach! Word-of-mouth is the oldest and most trusted form of marketing. When the right people talk, others listen.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.
skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

choices.label: C. Skip Marketing — Let the Talk Speak for Itself
choices.description: Focus entirely on making the talk exceptional. If the content is great, word will spread after the event.
choices.feedback: The purist's approach! Quality over hype. But in a world of infinite content, even brilliant ideas need help reaching ears.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Investing effort now for later payoff builds discipline.
skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. Collaborative Preview Event
choices.description: Organize a mini-talk jam with other TEDx speakers. Preview your best 3 minutes and build cross-promotion buzz.
choices.feedback: Community building! Collaboration beats competition. When speakers promote each other, the whole event benefits.

skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: One week until TEDx day. Everything comes together now — or falls apart. Coach TED gives you the final choice: 'You can't do everything this week. What matters most right now?'
rounds.goal: Make the critical final-week preparation decision.
rounds.coaching_moment: Risk tolerance: Last-minute decisions reveal your values. Do you chase perfection, seek safety, or bet on growth?
rounds.reflection_prompt: When time is running out, how do you decide what matters most?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Teenager in intense final rehearsal on school stage, clock showing deadline pressure, notes and script scattered, determined expression, dramatic lighting, semi-realistic

choices.label: A. Marathon Rehearsal Sessions
choices.description: Rehearse 4 hours a day for 7 days. By TEDx day, your talk will be muscle memory.
choices.feedback: The athlete's approach! Repetition builds confidence. But over-rehearsal can make your delivery robotic — keep the spark alive.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Resisting the quick fix in favor of lasting results shows maturity.
skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: B. Rewrite Your Opening 10 Times
choices.description: The first 30 seconds decide everything. Spend the entire week perfecting your hook.
choices.feedback: The opening is 80% of the battle! If you hook them in 30 seconds, you have them for 15 minutes. This is where most speakers fail.

skill_explanation.creativity: Combining ideas in unexpected ways shows innovative thinking.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. Mental Preparation & Visualization
choices.description: Spend the week on mental rehearsal: visualize success, practice breathing, build mental fortitude. Athletes call it 'the zone.'
choices.feedback: Elite performers visualize success before they achieve it. Mental preparation is the secret weapon most speakers ignore.

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: D. Rest and Trust Your Preparation
choices.description: You've worked for 10 weeks. Rest your voice, sleep well, and trust that you're ready. Freshness beats exhaustion.
choices.feedback: The wisdom of rest! Many speakers burn out in the final week. Trusting your preparation takes its own kind of courage.

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Evaluating risk vs. reward is a key life skill.

rounds.situation: This is it. The auditorium is full. 300 people. Spotlights. The red TEDx letters glow behind you. Your name is announced. You walk to center stage. The next 12 minutes will define everything you've worked for. How do you begin?
rounds.goal: Deliver your TEDx talk — the culmination of 12 weeks of preparation.
rounds.coaching_moment: This is the synthesis of everything: narrative, vulnerability, persuasion, stage presence, and audience connection. Trust yourself.
rounds.reflection_prompt: In this moment, what would you tell your Week 1 self? What have you learned about the power of your own voice?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Teenager confidently on TEDx school stage, red letters glowing, packed audience, spotlight, powerful speaking pose, emotional moment, semi-realistic

choices.label: A. Open with 10 Seconds of Silence
choices.description: Walk to center stage. Say nothing for 10 full seconds. Let the silence build unbearable tension. Then begin with a whisper.
choices.feedback: Masterful! Silence is the most confident thing a speaker can do. Those 10 seconds said: 'I own this stage. I'm in no rush. And what I'm about to say matters.'

skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Taking a calculated risk shows you can handle uncertainty.
skill_explanation.creativity: Not settling for the obvious solution builds creative problem-solving.
skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: B. Open with Your Most Personal Story
choices.description: Start with the vulnerable moment you've been preparing. No preamble. Drop the audience straight into the emotional core.
choices.feedback: You led with your heart, and the audience followed. When you shared that story, you could hear a pin drop. That's the power of authentic vulnerability.

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.
skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.
skill_explanation.creativity: Thinking outside the box leads to more original solutions.

choices.label: C. Open with a Provocative Question
choices.description: 'How many of you have ever...' Start with a question that makes every person in the room think 'yes, that's me.'
choices.feedback: Engagement from the first second! A great question makes the audience active participants. They're not watching a talk — they're part of it.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.
skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.

choices.label: D. Deliver Exactly What You Rehearsed
choices.description: Stick to the script. No improvisation. Trust your preparation and deliver the talk as practiced, word for word.
choices.feedback: Reliable and polished. You delivered exactly what you prepared, and the audience respected your preparation. Sometimes the safest path is the wisest one.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Waiting for the right moment instead of rushing shows self-control.
skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

glossary_terms.definition: The structure of a story from beginning through conflict to resolution. Great talks follow a narrative arc to keep audiences engaged.
The art of persuasive speaking and writing, dating back to ancient Greece. Includes logos (logic), pathos (emotion), and ethos (credibility).
The willingness to show uncertainty, risk, or emotional exposure. In public speaking, strategic vulnerability builds deep audience trust and connection.
A storytelling framework identified by Joseph Campbell: ordinary world, call to adventure, trials, transformation, and return. Used in everything from myths to TED talks.
A Greek rhetorical concept meaning 'the right moment.' In speaking, it means connecting your message to what feels urgent and relevant right now.
The ability to command attention through physical bearing, eye contact, vocal variety, and confident movement on stage.
The feeling that you don't deserve your success or position, despite evidence to the contrary. Common among speakers and high achievers.
Understanding how groups of people think, feel, and respond to messages. Includes attention spans, emotional triggers, social proof, and the bandwagon effect.

endings.title: TEDx Star
endings.message: Standing ovation. The crowd is on its feet. Teachers are wiping their eyes. Your talk wasn't just good — it was unforgettable. Every element clicked: the story hit home, the delivery was flawless, and the audience felt like you were speaking directly to each one of them. The TEDx organizers ask if they can upload it to the official channel. Within a week, it has 50,000 views. You didn't just give a talk — you created a moment that people will remember for years. You are a TEDx Star.

endings.title: Master Storyteller
endings.message: Your talk moved people. Truly moved them. A parent came up afterward with tears in their eyes: 'My child told me about your story and it changed how we talk at home.' Your narrative power was extraordinary — every scene painted, every emotion earned, every transition seamless. The writing was the star. You proved that in a world of flashy presentations, the ancient art of storytelling still reigns supreme. You are a Master Storyteller.

endings.title: Influence Builder
endings.message: Your talk went beyond the auditorium. It started conversations in hallways, sparked a student movement, and got shared across social media. The school principal invited you to speak at the district education conference. A local newspaper ran a feature on 'the 14-year-old who's changing how students think.' You didn't just give a talk — you built a platform. Your voice now carries weight far beyond that stage. You are an Influence Builder.

endings.title: Authentic Voice
endings.message: You might not have had the slickest slides or the most dramatic delivery. But something remarkable happened: you were REAL. When you stumbled on a line, you laughed. When your voice cracked telling your personal story, the audience leaned in closer. A classmate who never speaks up came to you afterward and said: 'You made me feel like it's okay to be myself.' That's worth more than any standing ovation. You found your Authentic Voice.

endings.title: Rising Speaker
endings.message: Your TEDx talk was a solid first effort. Was it perfect? No. Were there moments where you wished you'd prepared more, or been braver, or structured it differently? Sure. But here's what matters: you DID it. You stood on a stage, spoke your truth, and survived. Most people never do that. Coach TED smiled afterward and said: 'This was just the beginning. Your next talk will be twice as good.' You're a Rising Speaker — and the best is yet to come.
